title: Thermopylae: How Much of the Story Can We Trust?

chapters.title: Room for one wagon
chapters.text:
In the summer of 480 BC, a few thousand Greeks tried to stop the biggest army their world had ever seen. They chose a place where, says one ancient writer, the road had room for just one wagon. Why fight there? And how much of this famous story can we really trust?
Our main witness is Herodotus, a Greek writer who was only a small child when this war began. Years later, he travelled and asked people what they remembered. His book opens with a promise: so that things done by man not be forgotten in time.

chapters.title: The king who came west
chapters.text:
The invader was Xerxes, king of Persia, an empire that stretched from Egypt to India. In 480 BC he led his army out of Asia, across a narrow strait, and down the coast of Greece.
How big was that army? Herodotus gives a total of more than two and a half million fighting men. Most historians today think that is far too many, and that the real army was much smaller. Nobody knows the true number.
To hold the pass, the Greeks sent a little over five thousand men, plus fighters from nearby towns. Their leader was Leonidas, one of the two kings of Sparta.

chapters.title: Three days in the pass
chapters.text:
When Xerxes arrived, he waited four days, expecting the Greeks to run away. They did not. On the fifth day, he attacked.
For two days, his soldiers attacked the narrow pass, and for two days they failed. Even his best troops were thrown back. Herodotus calls them the Immortals: ten thousand men, always kept at full strength.
Then a local man named Ephialtes showed the Persians a mountain path that went around the pass. By the next morning, the Greeks were about to be surrounded.

chapters.title: Why the story lasted
chapters.text:
On that last day, Leonidas sent most of the army away. He stayed with his three hundred Spartans, and with the men of Thespiae and Thebes. Most of those who stayed were killed, Leonidas among them.
The Persians marched on. But later that year, their fleet lost at Salamis, and the next summer, their army lost at Plataea.
After the war, the Greeks set up stones at the pass. Herodotus copied the words written for the Spartans: Foreigner, go tell the Spartans that we lie here obedient to their commands.
And the pass? River mud has pushed the sea back by kilometres, and the road for one wagon is now a wide plain. Next time, we sail to Salamis, where the Persian fleet was beaten.
